Read About Düsseldorf

A working harbor turned design district, a fashion boulevard, and a rivalry with Cologne that never really ends — the smaller cousin on the Rhine that keeps outdressing everyone.

A Harbor That Reinvented Itself

Medienhafen — the "media harbor" where this guide's own hotel and its first day of stops sit — was a working cargo and grain port into the 1970s, lined with warehouses and cranes rather than restaurants and glass towers. As Rhine shipping consolidated elsewhere through the 1980s, the basin fell quiet, and Düsseldorf faced the choice every post-industrial harbor city eventually faces: let it decay, or gamble on it. The city chose to gamble, and unusually for Germany, it gambled on architecture as the draw. Frank Gehry was invited to build not one landmark but a cluster of three office buildings — the Neuer Zollhof, visible from nearly everywhere in the harbor — and other name architects followed: David Chipperfield, Claude Vasconi, Joe Coenen. What resulted is one of the few places in Germany where a reader can stand in one spot and see five or six genuinely different architectural statements arguing with each other, none of them older than thirty years.

The old cranes are mostly gone, but a few were kept standing deliberately — not as ruins, but as a reminder of what the harbor used to move.

The Rivalry That Runs on Beer

No German city takes its neighbor rivalry more seriously through a pint glass than Düsseldorf takes Cologne, forty kilometers south down the Rhine. The two cities have traded barbs for centuries over which is the more sophisticated Rhineland capital, but the argument crystallizes most visibly in what each city drinks. Düsseldorf brews Altbier — a dark, top-fermented beer served in small, straight 0.2-liter glasses that a waiter keeps refilling the instant one is empty, whether asked or not. Cologne brews Kölsch, a pale, delicate cousin served in similarly small glasses but with, Düsseldorf residents will insist, considerably less character. Order a Kölsch at an Altstadt brewpub and the staff will good-naturedly needle a visitor about it; the reverse holds in Cologne. It is a rivalry conducted almost entirely in good humor, but it is real, and the Altstadt's cluster of brewhouses — Uerige, Zum Schlüssel, Im Füchschen among them — are where it plays out nightly.

Little Tokyo, By Accident of Business

Immermannstraße and the streets around it hold one of Europe's largest concentrations of Japanese restaurants, grocers and businesses outside Japan itself — a district locals and visitors alike call Little Tokyo. It exists for a reason with nothing to do with tourism: after the Second World War, Mitsubishi and a wave of other Japanese trading and steel companies chose Düsseldorf as their European base, drawn by the Rhineland's industrial economy and its central position between the port of Rotterdam and the rest of the continent. Employees and their families followed, and by the 1960s a genuine Japanese community had taken root around the Hauptbahnhof. The restaurants that serve them today are not a themed district built for visitors — they are simply where a large expatriate community has always eaten, which is exactly why the ramen and sushi counters here are judged, by people who would know, among the most authentic in the country.

The city's Japanese School, still operating today, was founded in 1971 — a generation before "Little Tokyo" became a phrase anyone used to describe the neighborhood.

An Art City That Made Its Own Rules

Düsseldorf's claim to being a serious art city rests less on any single collection than on a teaching tradition. The Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, the city's art academy, produced or employed an outsized share of the artists who defined German art after 1945 — Joseph Beuys taught there for over a decade, developing his idea of "social sculpture" in direct dialogue with students who would themselves become major figures, among them Gerhard Richter, Sigmar Polke and Anselm Kiefer. That teaching lineage is part of why K20's own Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen holds one of the deepest Picasso collections outside Spain and France, and why Museum Kunstpalast, a few minutes away in the Ehrenhof, can move from classical antiquity to contemporary installation without the collection feeling like two separate museums stitched together. The city treats its art scene as infrastructure, not decoration — funded and maintained the way another city might fund its transit system.

The Village the City Grew Around

Kaiserswerth, the distant riverside stop that anchors this guide's third day, predates Düsseldorf itself by centuries. Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa built an imperial palace, the Kaiserpfalz, on the site in the 12th century, using it as a fortified customs post to control Rhine traffic — a strategic chokepoint long before "Düsseldorf" existed as a name on any map. The palace was destroyed in 1702 during the War of the Spanish Succession and was never rebuilt, leaving the roofless sandstone ruin that stands today. Kaiserswerth was its own independent town for most of its history and was only absorbed into Düsseldorf in 1929 — which is part of why it still feels distinct on arrival: a quiet, half-timbered riverside village that happens to share a postal code with a city of over 600,000 people.
